   Singapore’s first data centre under stricter green rules opens

 The Equinix SG6 data centre in Jalan Tukang opened on Nov 6.
 ST PHOTO: AZMI ATHNI
 Lee Li Ying
 Published   Nov 06, 2026, 08:25 PM
 Updated   Nov 06, 2026, 10:29 PM
 Set as preferred source Listen 中文 SINGAPORE – The first data centre built in Singapore under stricter green rules opened on Nov 6, as the country balances growing demand for computing power with energy and land constraints.
 US data centre operator Equinix invested US$290 million (S$370 million) in SG6, its sixth facility here. The nine-storey building in Jalan Tukang will initially accommodate about 1,550 server cabinets and provide 20 megawatts of computing capacity when fully built.
 SG6 is among four projects selected by the authorities after the lifting in 2022 of a three-year moratorium on new data centre developments, imposed to review how the sector could grow sustainably.
 The projects were assessed on sustainability, strategic contribution and economic value, rather than simply speed or scale.
 SG6 is designed to achieve a power usage effectiveness (PUE) ratio of 1.2, better than the ceiling of 1.3 required under the Government’s pilot Data Centre – Call for Application exercise.
 PUE measures how efficiently a data centre uses energy. A score that is closer to 1 indicates greater efficiency.
 Equinix said it aimed for 1.2 because it believed that level was achievable.
 To reduce energy use, the company worked with manufacturers to select efficient chillers, fine-tune pumps and size cooling equipment appropriately, getting more cooling from each unit of electricity.
 SG6 will also operate at about 27 deg C, compared with around 25 deg C at typical data centres. Allowing warmer temperatures reduces the energy needed to keep servers cool.
 The facility supports liquid cooling, which carries heat away from powerful computer chips more effectively than air.
 Such improvements matter in Singapore, where limited land, electricity and water constrain how much computing infrastructure can be added. 
 Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Tan Kiat How, who was guest of honour at the opening, said efficiency could create room for more digital activities despite resource constraints.
 “Singapore’s ambition is not maximum compute; it is maximum value from compute,” he said.
 A data centre’s value should be measured through the businesses it connects, the high-value computing tasks it supports, the capabilities it anchors and the innovation around it, he added.
 The facility supports artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and other data-intensive tasks. Equinix said it already has AI customers at SG6, but declined to identify them, citing business confidentiality.
 Tan also said SG6 is part of a larger digital infrastructure system taking shape across South-east Asia.
 “SG6 provides trusted, highly connected infrastructure for workloads that benefit from being in Singapore,” he said.
 SG6 will also host a research and testing facility developed with the National University of Singapore’s Energy Solutions Hub. Targeted to open in 2027, it will let researchers and companies trial technologies in a working data centre.
 The projects, intended as pilots lasting up to a year, will explore areas including liquid cooling, digital twins and battery energy storage.
 Digital twins are virtual models of physical equipment and systems. They can help operators test how changes to cooling or operating settings might affect performance before making adjustments in the actual facility.
 Liquid-cooling trials will explore ways to remove heat from increasingly powerful servers, while battery storage research will examine how stored electricity can support data centre operations.
 “Regulations set the baseline, but innovation must raise the ceiling,” Tan said, adding that successful solutions could subsequently be deployed across Singapore and the region.
 Digital and energy infrastructure together should increasingly be planned together, as data centres could account for about one-fifth of ASEAN’s growth in electricity demand between 2025 and 2030, he added.

 Countries bring complementary strengths: Some have more land and energy, while others offer large markets, industrial ecosystems or talent.
 Singapore contributes connectivity, capital, trusted institutions and a strong business ecosystem, with infrastructure suited to tasks where reliability, security and proximity to businesses matter, Tan said.
 “That is how I see Singapore’s contribution. Not to pull every workload here into Singapore, not to compete for every megawatt, but to help make the regional system work better.”
